meta.title: "A blogger recommends it": why being famous doesn't mean someone actually knows | Sila Slova
meta.description: Teach your child to separate popularity from competence and ask: "do they actually know this?". Game-based critical thinking course for children aged 8–12.

hero.headline: Does your child trust advice just because a "famous" person gives it?
hero.subheadline: "A blogger recommends it." "An athlete said so." "A star advertises it." It sounds convincing — because the person is successful. And your child trusts it automatically, without ever asking whether that person actually knows the subject.

media.alt: A child trusting advice because the person is famous, not because of their knowledge

pain.title: Being famous isn't being an expert
pain.body:
A person can sing beautifully, play football, or be popular online — but none of that says whether they know anything about health, money, studying, or whatever else they're recommending. Success in one thing doesn't make them an expert in everything.

This isn't being naive or gullible. The child is simply reacting to authority: if someone is famous and successful, it feels like they can be trusted. Without the habit of checking, any "famous" person automatically becomes a source of truth — even though they may know no more about the actual topic than anyone else.

The result — the child trusts the name, not the knowledge. They buy, repeat, and choose because "a star said so" — not because there's real competence behind the advice.

faq.q: What age is it suitable for?
